full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** This is not documented as a new form of spatial game chaos, and the "chaos" label is probably an artifact of the noise. The first pass was right about the noise but too generous in calling it a variant. Nothing in what was observed needs a new mechanism.

**1. The game is a snowdrift game, not a Prisoner's Dilemma.** With T=1.5 > R=1 > S=0.5 > P=0, the payoffs are in the snowdrift (hawk–dove) order. Hauert & Doebeli showed that in unstructured snowdrift games, intermediate levels of cooperation persist. Unexpectedly, spatial structure reduces the proportion of cooperators for a wide range of parameters. They also describe the spatial patterns: while in the spatial prisoner's dilemma cooperators can survive by forming large, compact clusters, in the spatial snowdrift game cooperators form only small filament-like clusters. That is, it is advantageous to adopt strategies that are opposite to neighboring strategies. Small, broken-up clusters fit the short correlation length (2) and the several small domains (about 5). Also, the well-mixed snowdrift equilibrium is (S−P)/[(S−P)+(T−R)] = 0.5/1.0 = **0.5 cooperators**. That would give a type entropy close to 1, which matches the observed 0.989. My reading is that the system behaves like a randomly mixed snowdrift population sitting at its textbook coexistence point.

**2. The mixing steps are a documented ingredient.** Copying a random neighbour every step (a voter-model step) or swapping with a neighbour at p=1.0 is very strong random mixing. Random movement in lattice games has been studied: one line of work used movement that was Brownian random walk like, i.e. diffusive, not relying on any type of explicit, genotypic or phenotypic assortment, and also being strategy-independent. Comparisons across games found that random migration plays the cooperation inhibiting role in spatial structures in the SDG, while playing the cooperation enhancing role in PDG and SHG. Vainstein & Arenzon present an extensive, systematic study of the Prisoner's Dilemma and Snowdrift games on a square lattice under a synchronous, noiseless imitation dynamics, including random mobility. Their setup is the closest published match to the SWAP and GAME versions in this class.

**3. Why the chaos test result is probably an artifact.** Nowak–May chaos is defined as a purely deterministic, spatial version of the Prisoners' Dilemma that produces chaotically changing spatial patterns. Here a random step (copy or swap at p=1.0) runs every step, so two copies of the run will drift apart in Hamming distance whatever the game does. Even work that measures chaos this way notes that in the case of the game exhibiting a degree of stochasticity, the distance increases more rapidly. That is why the test can't tell real chaos from plain noise here. The activity of 0.46 and the single reversal look like noise churning around a mixed equilibrium, not the shifting patterns Nowak and May described.

**Caveats:**
- **The g=(1.3, 0.0) member doesn't fit the snowdrift explanation.** With S=P it is the weak Prisoner's Dilemma, whose mixed-population outcome is all defectors. It still lands in the same fingerprint class, probably because the random step keeps both types around. That supports the idea that the noise sets the fingerprint, not the game. I can't confirm from here that it actually sits at the same roughly 50/50 split.
- **The domain count is ambiguous.** A value of about 5 could just as well describe random speckle; it isn't evidence of structure.
